resources.title: Gray wolf
resources.description: Identify Gray wolf, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Gray wolf (Canis lupus) can be identified as follows: Large canid with a broad muzzle, proportionally small rounded ears and a long, low-carried bushy tail; colour alone is unreliable. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

keyFacts.label: Range context
keyFacts.value: Canada Alaska and parts of contiguous United States

rangeSummary.value: Canada Alaska and parts of contiguous United States

identification.text: Large canid with a broad muzzle, proportionally small rounded ears and a long, low-carried bushy tail; colour alone is unreliable.

habitat.text: Forests, tundra, mountains and open country across much of Canada and Alaska.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Lives in packs, typically 6–7 (up to 20–30) animals, holding territories against other wolves
Howls to communicate, including warning other packs away
Preys mainly on moose, caribou or deer, with sheep, hares, beaver and other small prey
In the far northwest may follow migratory caribou; territories span hundreds to thousands of square kilometres

conservationStatus.text: The gray wolf, U.S.A.: All of AL, AR, CA, CO, CT, DE, FL, GA, IA, IN, IL, KS, KY, LA, MA, MD, ME, MI, MO, MS, NC, ND, NE, NH, NJ, NV, NY, OH, OK, PA, RI, SC, SD, TN, TX, VA, VT, WI, and WV; and portions of AZ, NM, OR, UT, and WA as follows: (1) Northern AZ (that portion north of the centerline of Interstate Highway 40); (2) Northern NM (that portion north of the centerline of Interstate Highway 40); (3) Western OR (that portion of OR west of the centerline of Highway 395 and Highway 78 north of Burns Junction and that portion of OR west of the centerline of Highway 95 south of Burns Junction); (4) Most of Utah (that portion of UT south and west of the centerline of Highway 84 and that portion of UT south of Highway 80 from Echo to the UT/WY Stateline); and (5) Western WA (that portion of WA west of the centerline of Highway 97 and Highway 17 north of Mesa and that portion of WA west of the centerline of Highway 395 south of Mesa). Mexico.: listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1978-03-09.
The gray wolf, U.S.A. (MN): listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 1978-03-09.

Mexican wolf (Canis lupus baileyi), Wherever found, except where included in an experimental population as set forth in 17.84(k): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1976-04-28.

resources.title: Eastern wolf
resources.description: Identify Eastern wolf, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern wolf (Canis lycaon) can be identified as follows: A medium-sized wolf of the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence region; appearance overlaps gray wolf and coyote, and visual identification may be inconclusive. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

keyFacts.label: Range context
keyFacts.value: Great Lakes and St. Lawrence forest region of Canada

taxonomicNotes.text: Authorities differ on eastern wolf taxonomy and ancestry; North Ground preserves the named entity and the uncertainty.

rangeSummary.value: Great Lakes and St. Lawrence forest region of Canada

identification.text: A medium-sized wolf of the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence region; appearance overlaps gray wolf and coyote, and visual identification may be inconclusive.

habitat.text: Forested landscapes of central Ontario and neighbouring Québec; taxonomy and hybrid ancestry are treated differently by authorities.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Lives in family packs; winter pack size in Algonquin Park has been recorded at 9-14.
Territories average roughly 190-200 km².
Preys on white-tailed deer, beaver and moose; some Algonquin wolves travel up to 42 km to follow deer to winter concentration areas.
Dens are usually in conifer-dominated forest near permanent water, in diggable soil such as sand.

resources.title: Coyote
resources.description: Identify Coyote, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Coyote (Canis latrans) can be identified as follows: Slender canid with a narrow muzzle, relatively large pointed ears and a bushy tail usually carried below the back. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Slender canid with a narrow muzzle, relatively large pointed ears and a bushy tail usually carried below the back.

habitat.text: Highly adaptable across forest, farmland, prairie and urban-edge landscapes.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Yelping, howling, high-pitched calls, especially at dusk and dawn; one howl sets off others, and two coyotes can sound like a dozen.
Primarily a flesh-eater that scavenges livestock carcasses and wolf kills and in suitable snow can kill deer.
Marks territory with strong-smelling urine.

resources.title: Red fox
resources.description: Identify Red fox, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Red fox (Vulpes vulpes) can be identified as follows: Usually red-orange with black legs, pointed ears and a white-tipped tail; silver and cross colour forms also occur. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

keyFacts.label: Range context
keyFacts.value: Native northern populations and introduced lineages in parts of North America

rangeSummary.value: Native northern populations and introduced lineages in parts of North America

identification.text: Usually red-orange with black legs, pointed ears and a white-tipped tail; silver and cross colour forms also occur.

habitat.text: Open woodland, farmland, tundra and urban-edge habitat across most of North America.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Mostly nocturnal or crepuscular and solitary, but territorial; families use a main earthen den.
Hunts rodents and rabbits with a high pounce; also eats birds, eggs, insects and plants.
Caches surplus food and revisits caches.
Vocal: howls, barks and whines.

conservationStatus.text: Sierra Nevada red fox (Vulpes vulpes necator), Sierra Nevada DPS: listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 2021-09-02.

resources.title: Gray fox
resources.description: Identify Gray fox, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus) can be identified as follows: Grizzled gray upperparts, rusty sides and a black stripe ending in a black tail tip distinguish it from red fox. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Grizzled gray upperparts, rusty sides and a black stripe ending in a black tail tip distinguish it from red fox.

habitat.text: Woodland and brushy habitat in the southern part of Canada and much of the United States.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: The only North American canid that climbs trees, using hooked claws to escape predators or reach food.
Mainly nocturnal and solitary outside breeding and pup rearing.
Dens in hollow trees and logs, rock crevices and burrows.
Omnivorous: small mammals, insects, birds and fruit (apples, berries, wild grapes); caches surplus food.

resources.title: Arctic fox
resources.description: Identify Arctic fox, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Arctic fox (Vulpes lagopus) can be identified as follows: Compact fox with small rounded ears and a very full tail; winter coats may be white or blue-gray and summer coats are brown-gray. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

keyFacts.label: Range context
keyFacts.value: Arctic tundra and northern coastal regions of North America

rangeSummary.value: Arctic tundra and northern coastal regions of North America

identification.text: Compact fox with small rounded ears and a very full tail; winter coats may be white or blue-gray and summer coats are brown-gray.

habitat.text: Arctic tundra and coastal environments north of the treeline.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Does not hibernate; nomadic and can travel several hundred kilometres.
Summer diet centres on lemmings and voles; also takes seabirds, eggs, berries and scavenges seal remains from polar bear kills.
Caches surplus food in summer; dens have 4–8 entrances and are dug in sandy banks, hillocks and talus.
Monogamous pairs raise pups together; families break up in September–October.

resources.title: Canada lynx
resources.description: Identify Canada lynx, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Canada lynx (Lynx canadensis) can be identified as follows: Long legs, very large furry feet, long black ear tufts and a short tail with a completely black tip. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

keyFacts.label: Range context
keyFacts.value: Boreal forest across Canada and Alaska with range into the northern contiguous United States

rangeSummary.value: Boreal forest across Canada and Alaska with range into the northern contiguous United States

identification.text: Long legs, very large furry feet, long black ear tufts and a short tail with a completely black tip.

habitat.text: Boreal forest strongly associated with snowshoe hare populations.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Solitary apart from breeding pairs and females with kittens, which sometimes hunt hares together in a line.
Hunts mainly at night, stalking or waiting in ambush.
Specialist predator of snowshoe hare, which can exceed 75% of the diet; lynx numbers cycle with hares roughly every 10 years.
Breeding season late February through March.

conservationStatus.text: The canada lynx, Wherever Found in Contiguous U.S.: listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 2000-03-24.

resources.title: Bobcat
resources.description: Identify Bobcat, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Bobcat (Lynx rufus) can be identified as follows: Short-tailed cat with barred forelegs and a tail tip that is black above and pale below; feet are smaller than a Canada lynx's. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Short-tailed cat with barred forelegs and a tail tip that is black above and pale below; feet are smaller than a Canada lynx's.

habitat.text: Forest, brush, rocky country and agricultural edges across southern Canada and the United States.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Solitary; sexes interact almost only in the breeding season.
Mostly nocturnal and crepuscular; terrestrial but a good climber.
Strictly carnivorous stalk-and-pounce hunter of mice, hares, squirrels, birds and deer fawns; can kill adult deer.
Marks territory with scent and yowls during the breeding season.

resources.title: Eastern cottontail
resources.description: Identify Eastern cottontail, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern cottontail (Sylvilagus floridanus) can be identified as follows: Compact brown-gray rabbit with a rusty nape and conspicuous white cotton-like tail; it does not turn white in winter. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Compact brown-gray rabbit with a rusty nape and conspicuous white cotton-like tail; it does not turn white in winter.

habitat.text: Brushy fields, hedgerows and suburban edges in eastern and central North America.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Rests by day in a 'form' concealed in dense grass, a brush pile or thicket, seldom far from cover.
Feeds almost entirely on plants: grasses, wheat and clovers; in deep snow eats buds, twigs, bark and sprouts.
Breeds mid-February through September; nests are shallow ground cavities lined with grass and fur.

resources.title: Arctic hare
resources.description: Identify Arctic hare, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Arctic hare (Lepus arcticus) can be identified as follows: Large northern hare with short ears and a winter-white coat; summer animals retain white feet and tail. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Large northern hare with short ears and a winter-white coat; summer animals retain white feet and tail.

habitat.text: Treeless Arctic tundra and rocky polar landscapes.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: When alarmed stands and hops on its hind legs, leaving tracks that look made by a three-legged animal; runs up to 64 km/h.
Mostly solitary but can gather in groups of 100 or more, with one animal staying alert while others rest.
Willow makes up about 95% of the diet, plus saxifrage, crowberry, dryas, grasses, lichens and mosses; digs through snow to feed.

resources.title: American red squirrel
resources.description: Identify American red squirrel, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: American red squirrel (Tamiasciurus hudsonicus) can be identified as follows: Small reddish squirrel with a pale eye ring and whitish belly; it is much smaller than an eastern gray squirrel. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Small reddish squirrel with a pale eye ring and whitish belly; it is much smaller than an eastern gray squirrel.

habitat.text: Coniferous and mixed forests across northern North America.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Active by day and noisy: rattles, screeches, growls, buzzes and chirps used to defend territories year-round.
Harvests conifer cones in late summer and autumn and stores them in central middens; cone cuttings on stumps and rocks are common sign.
Eats mainly conifer seeds plus many mushrooms, buds, fruit, sap, insects and occasionally bird eggs or young snowshoe hares.

resources.title: Eastern gray squirrel
resources.description: Identify Eastern gray squirrel, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern gray squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis) can be identified as follows: Medium tree squirrel, usually gray with a white belly and large bushy tail; black colour morphs are common in parts of Canada. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

keyFacts.label: Range context
keyFacts.value: Eastern North America with introductions in west

rangeSummary.value: Eastern North America with introductions in west

identification.text: Medium tree squirrel, usually gray with a white belly and large bushy tail; black colour morphs are common in parts of Canada.

habitat.text: Deciduous and mixed woodland, parks and urban areas in eastern North America.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Very vocal: squalls, warning barks, chucks and tooth chattering, often with tail flicks
Staples are acorns and other nuts, plus buds, fruit, fungi and corn
Breeds twice a year (December–February and May–June); nests in cavities or leaf nests
Mass movements can follow nut-crop failure or high populations

resources.title: North American beaver
resources.description: Identify North American beaver, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: North American beaver (Castor canadensis) can be identified as follows: Large aquatic rodent with a broad flat scaly tail, webbed hind feet and orange incisors. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Large aquatic rodent with a broad flat scaly tail, webbed hind feet and orange incisors.

habitat.text: Ponds, lakes, rivers and wetlands where woody vegetation is available.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Slaps the tail on the water as a warning
Fells trees (on average hundreds a year, up to about 40 cm diameter) for food and building
Builds dams, lodges and bank dens; castor from glands near the tail is used for scent marking
Usually stays within about 0.8 km of its den; two-year-olds disperse

resources.title: Raccoon
resources.description: Identify Raccoon, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Raccoon (Procyon lotor) can be identified as follows: Stocky mammal with a black facial mask and a ringed tail. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Stocky mammal with a black facial mask and a ringed tail.

habitat.text: Woodland, wetlands, farmland and urban areas, usually near water or cover.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Mainly nocturnal; family groups forage together at night and den by day
Omnivorous: crayfish, corn, fruit, nuts, eggs, insects; raids garbage in towns
In the north dens through winter on stored fat (not true hibernation)
Handles food with the front paws, the source of the 'washing' reputation

resources.title: American mink
resources.description: Identify American mink, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: American mink (Neogale vison) can be identified as follows: Long, low dark-brown mustelid with a narrow tail and a small white chin patch; substantially smaller than a river otter. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Long, low dark-brown mustelid with a narrow tail and a small white chin patch; substantially smaller than a river otter.

habitat.text: Shorelines, marshes and wooded waterways across North America.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Mostly nocturnal, especially near dawn and dusk; movements are quick and erratic.
Solitary; marks territory with anal-gland secretions and can discharge a foul-smelling liquid when threatened.
Strong swimmer that dives to about 5 m; dens in riverbank burrows or dens taken over from other mammals.
Eats crayfish and frogs in summer and small mammals (including muskrats), fish and waterfowl year-round, with mammals dominating winter diet.

resources.title: Fisher
resources.description: Identify Fisher, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Fisher (Pekania pennanti) can be identified as follows: Large dark mustelid with a long body, pointed face and long bushy tapering tail. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Large dark mustelid with a long body, pointed face and long bushy tapering tail.

habitat.text: Mature and regenerating forest across northern North America.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Opportunistic carnivore hunting on the forest floor and in the canopy: squirrels, chipmunks, mice, porcupines, plus insects, fruit and fungi.
One of the few predators that regularly kills porcupines.
Kits born late February to May, typically March–April, in tree cavities.

conservationStatus.text: The fisher, Southern Sierra Nevada Distinct Population Segment: listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 2020-06-15.

resources.title: American marten
resources.description: Identify American marten, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: American marten (Martes americana) can be identified as follows: Slender mustelid with rounded ears, a bushy tail and a yellow-orange throat bib. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Slender mustelid with rounded ears, a bushy tail and a yellow-orange throat bib.

habitat.text: Coniferous and mixed forests with structural cover across northern North America.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

activityContexts.note: This species may be managed under trapping or furbearer frameworks; identity does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Usually solitary and mostly nocturnal, hunting most at dusk and dawn; active all winter and does not hibernate.
Moves easily in trees and scent-marks trails from tree to tree, but does most hunting on the ground; also swims well.
Eats mainly small mammals such as squirrels and other rodents, plus birds, fruit, nuts, insects and carrion.
Dens in hollow trees, crevices or vacant burrows.
